newsitem.title: UK: U.S., Europe worry over Turkey as tension grows.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Europe worry over Turkey as tension grows.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Washington and its European allies are increasingly worried by signs that Turkey, a vital strategic partner, may be turning away from the West -- at a time of growing Greek-Turkish tension over the divided island of Cyprus.

Diplomats say meetings planned in the next few days and weeks will try to assess the risks of a major new crisis in southern Europe and just how far Turkey, frustrated by its relations with the European Union, is prepared to change course.

A decision by Cyprus to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles has raised the temperature at the worst possible time, with diplomats trying to push a U.N.-sponsored peace plan for the island and hoping for a breakthrough.
Turkey, whose troops occupy the northern part of Cyprus, is already bitterly disappointed at the lack of progress in its relations with the 15-nation European Union.

Ankara blames Greece for blocking promised European Union economic help although there is also EU concern over Turkey's human rights record. Greece can block the aid because it is a member of the EU, while Turkey is not. Both countries are NATO members.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Tuesday that Turkey was turning towards closer ties with Moslem neighbours.

"Turkey feels that it is wrongly treated by Europe," he told reporters. "How can one hold this against Turkey? Ankara has not profited by one penny from the customs union with the EU because Greece puts the brakes on everything."

Some diplomats say Turkey -- an important ally for the West because it borders volatile regions of the Caucasus and the Middle East -- could block NATO decisions in retaliation, including the alliance's planned enlargement to Eastern Europe.

"There has been talk of the Turks taking a really hard line because of what has happened. The warnings have been there before but there may be reason to take it more seriously now," said one European diplomat.

Ankara has said the Cyprus missile purchase is unacceptable and that it would not tolerate a change in the balance of power with Greece in the eastern Mediterranean. In diplomatic terms, that language clearly leaves open the option of using force.

The two NATO allies have gone to the brink of war several times, most recently last year in a territorial dispute in the Aegean. Four people also died in a series of clashes between the divided communities on Cyprus last year.
The island has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded and occupied its northern third after a coup engineered by the military government which ruled Greece at the time.

Washington and its allies have criticised Cyprus for the planned missile purchase, which they see as threat to peace hopes. The clock is ticking because Cyprus is due to start negotiations, probably in 1998, on joining the European Union.
The United States announced on Tuesday it would send a senior official to the island this weekend, after U.S. officials meet their European counterparts in the Hague on Friday.

There is much sensitivity over how to tackle the problems between Greece and Turkey, not least because Richard Holbrooke -- the U.S. negotiator who clinched the Bosnia peace deal -- accused the Europeans last year of failing to deal with them.
European diplomats said the Hague meeting would try to ensure the United States was coordinating its efforts with others and continuing to back the U.N. proposals for Cyprus.
"There is some concern that the Americans might be preparing a Holbrooke-style offensive for Cyprus all on their own, and we think that would be counterproductive," said one envoy.

Another meeting of European countries, set for January 29 in Rome, will address the broader question of how to handle Turkey. Diplomats said many EU states were impatient with Greece and had urged it to take an easier line with Ankara.

Turkey has long wanted to join the European Union but has received no firm promises, while a string of other countries from the Mediterranean and Eastern Europe have now officially joined the queue for membership.
Moreover, Turkey was angered by what it saw as Western inaction in Bosnia and NATO's failure to accept its concerns over arms control agreements with Russia.

The long tradition of secular, Western-oriented government in Turkey, which is overwhelmingly Moslem, has come under increasing strain as a result. The coalition government is led by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, an Islamist.
Erbakan hosted a meeting of ministers from eight Moslem countries in Istanbul last weekend, aimed at boosting economic cooperation among them.

Iran, seen as a major threat by the United States, attended the meeting. To Washington's annoyance, Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani recently visited Turkey and Ankara signed a $23 billion agreement for the supply of Iranian natural gas.
